adversarial_test_results.prompt: Captain Elena Marsh had chased rumors of the sunken Meridian light for eleven seasons across grey northern waters. Her crew, a stubborn mix of cartographers, divers, welders, believed the old charts hid a second passage behind Gull Rock. Storms met them past the skerries, fog swallowed the bowsprit, gulls vanished for days. Marsh kept her log in blunt pencil strokes, marking each failed sounding, each snapped cable, each cold meal eaten standing up. On the ninth morning the sonar sang out, sharp, certain, alive, and the whole deck held its breath. Divers went down through green silence, lamps trembling, bubbles rising like slow silver coins. Below them lay a hull split open across black sand, masts fallen, chains curled like sleeping snakes. Among scattered crates they found brass bells, porcelain cups, letters tied with string, a captain's clock stopped at midnight. Back aboard, soaked, laughing, weeping, the crew spread the salvage across the deck while Marsh recorded every item. The log entry ran long (her hand cramped around the pencil), and nobody slept until the stars burned through the clearing sky.
